say: You give it two points. It finds the point exactly halfway between them, the **midpoint**.
The key idea: halfway is the average. Average the x-values, then average the y-values.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a short step inside bigger Paper 2 coordinate geometry questions, for example the midpoint of a segment whose end has unknown coordinates.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it directly on Paper 2, as a 5-mark part, often to find the centre of a circle from the ends of a diameter.

steps.title: Average the x-values
steps.say: Add the two x-values and halve. This gives the x of the midpoint.

steps.title: Average the y-values
steps.say: Do the same with the y-values. This gives the y of the midpoint.

steps.title: Write the point
steps.say: Put the $\hl{1}{x}$ and the $\hl{2}{y}$ together as a point.

lines.text: Check: $2$ is exactly halfway between $-4$ and $8$.

higher.tip: Even if you do not finish, using the midpoint of the segment earns marks, so write the midpoint down first.

ordinary.tip: Write the midpoint formula with some numbers put in. That alone earns marks.
Substitute fully into the formula. A fully substituted formula moves you to high partial credit.
Leaving the answer as a fraction only earns partial credit. Simplify each coordinate.
A correct answer with no work can earn full marks, but one slip then leaves nothing to credit. Show the substitution.

say: You give it two points on a line. It tells you the **slope**, how steep the line is.
The key idea: slope is rise over run. Divide the change in $y$ by the change in $x$.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a step inside larger Paper 2 coordinate geometry questions, for example to get the slope of a radius, a tangent or the angle between two lines.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it directly on Paper 2, most years as a 5-mark part, and then often uses it in a 10-mark equation of a line.

example.question: Find the slope of the line through $P(-2, 1)$ and $Q(4, 10)$.

steps.title: Write the formula
steps.say: Slope is the change in $y$ over the change in $x$. Take $P$ first and $Q$ second, in the same order top and bottom.

lines.text: Subtract in the same order on top and bottom.

steps.title: Put the numbers in
steps.say: Put in the $y$-values on top and the $x$-values on the bottom.

steps.title: Simplify
steps.say: Work out top and bottom, then divide both by 3.

higher.tip: Marks are given for substituting into the slope formula, even if you stop there.
When a tangent is asked for, the slope of the tangent is its own marked step. Get it before the equation of the line.

sources.quote: Step 2. Finds slope of the tangent

ordinary.tip: Write the slope formula down first. It earns low partial credit on its own.
Fully substitute the formula. Then even a slip in the arithmetic still earns high partial credit.
An error in a substitution that you then finish correctly still earns marks, so keep going.

sources.quote: Error(s) in substitution but finishes correctly

ordinary.tip: If you are asked to tick a box, tick it. Correct work without it loses a mark.

sources.quote: Fully correct work but box not ticked

say: You give it a line and a point. It tells you whether the point is **on** the line, and where the line meets the axes.
The key idea: a point is on a line when its coordinates make the equation true. For an axis, one coordinate is $0$.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a step inside Paper 2 coordinate geometry, often a 5-mark part checking a point on a line, or finding an intercept for an area.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level uses it in 5-mark and 10-mark parts on Paper 2: test a point in the equation, or find where the line crosses an axis.

example.question:
The line $l$ has equation $3x - 2y - 12 = 0$.
(i) Show that $(6, 3)$ is on $l$.
(ii) Find where $l$ crosses the x-axis and the y-axis.

steps.title: Test the point
steps.say: A point is on the line if its coordinates make the equation true. Put $x = 6$ and $y = 3$ into the left side.

lines.text: The left side equals $0$, so $(6, 3)$ is on $l$.

steps.title: Cross the x-axis
steps.say: On the x-axis, $\hl{1}{y = 0}$. Put that in and solve for $x$.

lines.text: The line crosses the x-axis at $(4, 0)$.

steps.title: Cross the y-axis
steps.say: On the y-axis, $\hl{3}{x = 0}$. Put that in and solve for $y$.

lines.text: The line crosses the y-axis at $(0, -6)$.

higher.tip: To check a point, substitute it into the equation. Some substitution earns low partial credit, a full one earns high.

sources.quote: Some substitution into equation of line

higher.tip: A full substitution of the point into the equation of the line is what takes you to high partial credit.
Finding the intercepts is marked as separate steps, one for each axis. Do both.

ordinary.tip: When you show a point is on a line, end with the line $0 = 0$. It is how the scheme shows it is true.
Give an intercept as a pair of co-ordinates, not just a number. A bare number loses a mark.

sources.quote: Answer not given as a pair of co-ordinates

ordinary.tip: Putting $y = 0$ and finding $x$ earns high partial credit on its own.

sources.quote: Substitutes 𝑦= 0 and correctly finds 𝑥

say: You give it two points. It finds the **distance** between them, the length of the segment.
The key idea: the two points are the ends of the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle. The sides are the differences in $x$ and in $y$, so use Pythagoras.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a step inside Paper 2 circle questions: the distance between centres, or from a centre to a point, then a comparison with the radii.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it directly on Paper 2, as a 5-mark or 10-mark part, often to find a radius or the length of a side.

steps.title: Find the two differences
steps.say: Subtract the x-values, then subtract the y-values. These are the two sides of the right-angled triangle.

steps.title: Use the distance formula
steps.say: Square the $\hl{1}{x}$ difference and the $\hl{2}{y}$ difference, add them, and take the square root.

lines.text: If the root does not come out whole, leave it as a surd like $\sqrt{52}$.

higher.tip: In circle questions the distance between the centres is a marked step. Find it, then compare it with the radii.
End with a conclusion. A missing or wrong conclusion loses a mark.

sources.quote: Apply a * if there is no conclusion or an

ordinary.tip: Write the distance formula with some numbers in. That earns partial credit even if you go no further.
Substitute the formula correctly. If you slip but finish correctly, you still earn high partial credit.

sources.quote: Error(s) in substitution but finishes correctly

ordinary.tip: You may leave the answer as a surd. Both forms are accepted for full marks.
